newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich wrestles with decision on ethics payment.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich wrestles with decision on ethics payment.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich met with his lawyers and staff Wednesday on how to pay a $300,000 penalty stemming from his reprimand on ethics charges but no decision was made, his office said.

The issue has been a cloud over Gingrich's political future since January when the House voted 395-28 to reprimand him and impose the penalty to defray some of the costs of a two-year ethics investigation.

As rumours of an imminent announcement swirled through the Capitol, the speaker's spokeswoman Christina Martin told reporters: "No decision has been made. He cannot reach a decision until we have resolved the final outstanding issues and I don't know how long that will take."
She said she did not expect an announcement Wednesday.
Speculation that Gingrich was about to announce his plan to pay the penalty flared in advance of a closed-door meeting with his Republican colleagues before the House began its Wednesday session.
But Gingrich merely told party members that no decision had been made and that he would brief them when he had reached a decision.

Martin said that a "dialogue" on the penalty was under way with members and staff of the House ethics committee. The committee is currently in a moratorium and only the chairman and vice chairman have been appointed.

How Gingrich pays will be critical to his new intensive efforts to repair his image and reaffirm leadership of his party. He is under heavy pressure not to use campaign funds but to use his personal money -- even if he has to take out a loan. The speaker has an annual salary of $171,500.

Gingrich was the House's biggest fund-raiser in the last election cycle, with net receipts of more than $6.2 million, according to newly released Federal Election Commission figures, and using campaign money would make the penalty relatively painless.
"I have said from Day One that the speaker should pay the fine," Republican Representative Christopher Shays of Connecticut said.
"However outrageous I think it was, the bottom line is that he agreed to it," Shays said. "If he doesn't pay this personally, this does become a problem for him."
Shays said Gingrich was not a wealthy person and might have to borrow the money.
Representative John Boehner of Ohio, a member of the House Republican leadership team, said: "He's got to decide. I think it's up to Newt."

Gingrich has also been reported to have considered the option of launching a legal defence fund -- but this course also would spark criticism, although Gingrich would be able to point to President Clinton's use of such a fund to pay legal bills.

Gingrich has been working hard to repair his image and his ties to the conservative wing of the party. He won favourable press reviews with a trip to China and has been making numerous public appearances in recent days.
